source.title: A loss-based patch label denoising method for improving whole-slide image analysis using a convolutional neural network
source.authors: Murtaza Ashraf; Willmer Rafell Quiñones Robles; Mujin Kim; Young-Sin Ko; Mun Yong Yi

record.file_problem: Full text supplied; no apparent cut-off or garbling that prevents review.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies synthetic label noise in a pathology image dataset and evaluates training accuracy-related performance, but evaluates LossDiff denoising against a baseline rather than testing the original random-label memorization protocol.
record.gate_note: The PatchCamelyon experiments report performance across 10%, 20%, 30% and 40% randomly flipped labels. These results bear on V4's noisy-label setting, but the reported measure is accuracy, not training-set fit or test error. No experiments test completely random labels, unstructured inputs, explicit regularization, or learning order. Architecture selection results in Table 5 are preliminary model-selection results, not results on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses noisy-label memorization and overfitting to motivate LossDiff, but evaluates denoising and classification performance. It does not measure fitting corrupted training labels, complete random-label memorization, or the learning order of clean and noisy examples. Table 8's accuracy degradation alone does not establish V4's joint training-fit and generalization behavior.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that patch label noise harms CNN classification and that LossDiff improves patch-level stomach-image classification and robustness to induced PatchCamelyon label noise. They do not establish random-label memorization or clean-before-noise learning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained DenseNet-201 with Adam and synthetic labels flipped to the opposite class on PatchCamelyon, then applies LossDiff sample discarding or label flipping. This is a noisy-label robustness and denoising experiment, not the original random-label memorization protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Accuracy varies with the synthetic noise percentage and with LossDiff configuration (sample discarding versus label flipping).

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline accuracy declines from 84.23% to 69.33% as opposite-class label flips increase from 10% to 40%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing synthetic label noise reduces reported PatchCamelyon classification accuracy in this training and evaluation protocol.

fits_no_version.finding: At 40% noise, sample discarding achieves 79.67% accuracy and label correction 77.13%, versus 69.33% for baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LossDiff improves classification accuracy under synthetic label noise; sample discarding performs better than label correction at 20%–40% noise, but not at 10%.

record.problems: Table 8 reports accuracy without specifying whether it is training or test accuracy. The experiment adds synthetic noise only through 40%, and does not test perfect fitting of random labels or chance-level test error. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these values.
record.rows_left_out: None. Table 8 results are included by noise level and method; the text's separate 10% advantage statement is included as R13 and overlaps the table result.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence time as corruption increases. Figure 12 compares denoising methods instead.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across corruption levels together with steadily increasing clean-test error toward chance. Only classification accuracy at 10%–40% label flips is reported, without a clear evaluation-label protocol.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy labels. Figure 5 compares aggregate training and validation losses with and without cleaning; it does not track clean and noisy examples separately.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the proposed V4 limits_scope verdict: missing measurements are untested components, not evidence of a scope limitation. The statement that labels are flipped in each distribution leaves evaluation-label corruption ambiguous. Neither aggregate overfitting in Figure 5 nor comparisons of denoising training times supply the missing claim-specific measurements.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random training labels; no report of zero or near-zero training error or chance test error under random labels.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or convergence as the corrupted-label fraction grows.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiments.

Does not report whether either model fits the training set perfectly at each noise level or whether test error rises steadily toward chance; tested synthetic label noise only through 40%, not all labels.
No random-label experiments with or without weight decay, dropout or data augmentation.
No measurement of the learning order for real patterns and noisy or random labels.

rows.value: 10% better accuracy than the baseline method
rows.locator: Results, Noise handling ability analysis; Discussion
rows.note: Authors describe this as a 10% better accuracy advantage; Table 8 gives the underlying values, but the text does not specify whether this is percentage points or relative percent.
rows.check: Duplicate summary of R10 and R11, not an independent result. Their difference is 10.34 percentage points; it is a denoising benefit, not a random-label fitting measure.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: PatchCamelyon, 10%–40% synthetic label noise; LossDiff sample discarding and label flipping
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy falls as corruption rises for all three methods, but the reported measure does not establish perfect training fit or test error approaching chance; LossDiff accuracy remains higher than baseline at each listed level (R1–R13).
